blocks.prompt: The Snail That Cannot Leave Its House
blocks.text: A snail was born with its shell. The shell was tiny and soft. Then the snail ate chalky bits of dirt, and the shell grew hard. It grew round and round in a curl. The snail cannot take the shell off. The shell is part of the snail, the way your fingernail is part of you. When rain comes, the snail comes out. It puts out two long stalks. Its eyes are on the tips. If you touch a stalk, the snail pulls the eye back inside, like a sock turning inside out. Then it pushes the eye out again and keeps going.

blocks.prompt: The Slowest Mouth Full of Teeth
blocks.text: A snail has no legs. It has one foot, and the foot is the whole bottom of its body. To move, the snail sends a ripple down that foot, from the back to the front, over and over. Each ripple pushes it forward a tiny bit. This is why a snail looks like it is floating. It is really walking, just very slowly. A garden snail is one of the slowest animals on Earth. At a snail race in England, the champion crossed thirteen inches in two minutes. Now look inside its mouth. A snail does not have one soft tongue. It has a ribbon covered in teeth, and the ribbon works like sandpaper. A garden snail can have around fourteen thousand tiny teeth on it. The snail scrapes the ribbon across a leaf and shaves off little pieces. When the front teeth wear down, the ribbon moves forward and new teeth take their place. The snail never runs out.

answers: one foot, and it is the whole bottom of its body
it sends ripples down its foot from back to front
a ribbon covered in thousands of tiny teeth
(inference: the front teeth wear down from scraping, so new ones keep replacing them)

notes: The mantle is the flap that builds the shell

blocks.prompt: The House That Grows With You
blocks.text: A snail shell is not a helmet the snail found and climbed into. The snail builds it, and it never stops building. Behind the snail's head is a flap of skin called the mantle. The mantle pulls calcium out of the snail's food, turns it into calcium carbonate, the same hard stuff in chalk and in seashells, and lays it down along the open lip of the shell. So the shell grows outward from the middle. The point at the tip is the shell the snail wore the day it hatched. The rim near its head is what it built last week. A snail cannot outgrow its shell and move into a bigger one, because the shell is attached to its body by muscle. Take a snail out of its shell and you do not free it. You kill it. Now look closely at the curl. Almost every garden snail coils to the right. Hold one with the point up and the opening will face right. Now and then a snail hatches that coils the other way. In 2016 a left-coiling garden snail was found in a compost heap in London and became famous. Scientists named him Jeremy and searched the country for another lefty, because a left-coiling snail and a right-coiling snail cannot line up well enough to mate. News stories at the time put the odds of being born backward at about one in a million.

answers: a flap of skin behind the head that builds the shell out of calcium carbonate
new shell is only added at the open lip, so the middle was built first
the shell is attached to its body by muscle, so it is part of the animal
(inference: left-coiling snails are extremely rare, about one in a million)

notes: Slime is glue at rest and liquid under pressure

blocks.prompt: The Animal That Walks on Glue
blocks.text: A snail leaves a silver line behind it on the path. That line is the reason a snail can do almost anything. Snail slime is one substance doing two opposite jobs. Sit still on it and it behaves like a glue, thick and sticky enough to hold the whole animal against gravity. Push on it hard and it thins out and flows like a liquid. Engineers call this shear thinning. It is the same trick that makes toothpaste sit in a blob until you squeeze the tube. The snail squeezes its slime with the waves of muscle running down its foot. Where the foot presses, the slime turns runny and the snail slides forward. Where the foot rests, the slime sets and grips. That is how a snail hangs upside down under a wet leaf without falling, and how it climbs a pane of glass. It is also why a snail can cross a sharp edge unhurt. It is not really touching the edge. It is riding on a thin layer of its own slime. The slime does one more job. When the weather turns dry, a snail pulls in, seals the mouth of its shell with a lid of hardened mucus called an epiphragm, and waits. It can wait a long time. In 1846 a museum in London glued a desert snail to a display card, assuming it was dead. Four years later somebody noticed a fresh trail on the card. They put the snail in warm water, and it woke up, walked out, and started eating. Doctors are paying attention. A surgical glue inspired by the slime of a slug, a snail's close cousin, has been tested to seal wounds on a beating heart. It sticks to wet, moving tissue where ordinary tape slides off. Making slime is expensive. A snail spends a large share of its energy on the trail it leaves behind, which is one reason it never hurries. Some snails save effort by gliding along a trail another snail has already laid down.

6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Snail That Cannot Leave Its House

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Gastropod: Greek for stomach and foot
The shell follows a logarithmic spiral
The radula is a tooth-covered feeding ribbon
Limpet teeth are strengthened with goethite
Cone snails fire a hollow tooth like a harpoon
Ziconotide: a painkiller made from cone snail venom

blocks.prompt: Slow, Armored, and Armed: What a Snail Really Is
blocks.text: Start with the word. A snail is a gastropod, from Greek roots meaning stomach and foot, because early naturalists looked at one and decided it was an animal walking on its belly. They were close enough. A snail is a soft, unsegmented body that solved three problems at once: how to carry armor you can never take off, how to eat things harder than you are, and, in one branch of the family, how to hunt animals far faster than you when you travel at an inch a minute. The armor comes first. A snail's shell is secreted, not found. A sheet of tissue called the mantle pulls calcium and carbonate out of the snail's food and blood and lays down crystal along the growing lip. Because material is only ever added at the opening, the shell can only spiral, and it does so in a shape mathematicians call a logarithmic spiral, in which each turn is a scaled copy of the one before. This is efficient design. The snail never has to remodel what it already built, and the house always fits, because it grows at exactly the rate its owner does. The cost is that the shell is bone of its bone. Pull a snail from its shell and you have not evicted it. You have gutted it. The mouth comes second. A snail has no jaws worth the name. It has a radula, a flexible ribbon studded with thousands of microscopic teeth, which it drags across its food like a rasp. A garden snail carries roughly fourteen thousand of them, and as the leading rows wear away the ribbon advances and fresh teeth arrive from behind, a conveyor belt of dentistry. Related gastropods have pushed this tool to extremes. Limpets grip rock with teeth reinforced by goethite, a mineral fiber that ranks among the strongest biological materials ever measured. The weapon comes third, and here the story stops being gentle. Cone snails live in tropical seas, and some of them hunt fish. A fish is thousands of times faster than a snail, so the snail does not chase it. It waits, extends a long tube, and fires a single hollow radular tooth like a harpoon, loaded with venom. That venom is a cocktail of small proteins called conotoxins, each one shaped to jam a specific channel or receptor in a nerve cell. The fish does not slow down. It stops, mid-flick, and the snail reels it in. A few cone snail species carry venom strong enough to kill a person, and there is no antivenom. Then the turn. Because conotoxins interfere with nerve signals so precisely, pharmacologists began reading cone snail venom as a chemical library rather than a threat. One compound from Conus magus, a fish-hunting cone snail, became a drug called ziconotide, approved in the United States in 2004. It blocks a calcium channel that carries pain signals up the spinal cord. By weight it is dramatically more potent than morphine, and unlike morphine it is not an opioid, so it does not create the same dependence. A slow predator on a reef had spent millions of years solving a problem human chemists were still working on. That is the honest shape of a snail. Not a cute, slow thing with a house on its back. An old, patient design: armored, armed, and far better engineered than it looks.
